title: Chapter 2 Mastery Quiz: Biological Bases of Behavior
description: Test your mastery of neurons, neurotransmitters, nervous system architecture, and cerebral functions.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the myelin sheath that covers many neuronal axons?

options.text: To insulate the axon and dramatically increase the speed of electrical conduction
To absorb toxic waste products from the blood
To permanently attach neurons directly to muscle fibers

questions.explanation: Myelin acts as an electrical insulator, enabling rapid saltatory conduction across nodes of Ranvier.

questions.question: What is the typical resting membrane potential of an inactive mammalian neuron?
questions.explanation: At rest, the interior of a neuron maintains a negative electrical charge of approximately -70 millivolts.

questions.question: During the initial rising depolarization phase of an action potential, which ions rush rapidly INTO the intracellular space?
questions.explanation: When threshold is breached, voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na+ ions surge in down their electrochemical gradient.

questions.question: The 'All-or-None' principle dictates that:

options.text: A neuron generates an action potential at full amplitude or not at all
All neurons in a brain lobe must fire simultaneously
Every neurotransmitter is released in equal proportions
Axons only fire when stimulated by dopamine

questions.explanation: Once threshold is reached, an action potential fires with standard invariant voltage regardless of stimulus magnitude.

questions.question: Which neurotransmitter plays a central role in neuromuscular contractions and is severely depleted in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine operates at neuromuscular junctions and supports memory formation in the hippocampus.

questions.question: Dopamine hypofunction in the substantia nigra produces the motor tremors and rigidity characteristic of which disorder?
questions.explanation: Parkinson's is caused by the progressive death of dopamine-producing neurons in the midbrain substantia nigra.

questions.question: What is the primary INHIBITORY neurotransmitter in the central nervous system that calms neural firing?
questions.explanation: GABA hyperpolarizes postsynaptic membranes, reducing the likelihood of action potentials.

questions.question: A psychoactive drug that mimics or amplifies the natural effect of a neurotransmitter is termed a(n):
questions.explanation: Agonists fit into receptors and stimulate neural activity just like the body's natural neurotransmitters.

questions.question: Which division of the autonomic nervous system produces pupil dilation, elevated heart rate, and bronchial dilation during an emergency?
questions.explanation: The sympathetic system mobilizes physiological reserves for fight-or-flight reactions.

questions.question: Which hindbrain structure controls involuntary vital functions including respiration, heart rate, and blood pressure?
questions.explanation: The medulla sits directly above the spinal cord and sustains vital autonomic cardiovascular and respiratory reflexes.

questions.question: A gymnast who displays exceptional balance and refined motor coordination relies heavily on which brain region?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary motor routines, posture, balance, and procedural motor sequencing.

questions.question: All sensory modalities except which one pass through the Thalamus before reaching the cerebral cortex?
questions.explanation: Olfactory projections bypass the thalamus and project directly to the olfactory bulb and limbic structures.

questions.question: Which limbic structure is famously known as the key hub for processing fear, threat appraisal, and emotional salience?
questions.explanation: The amygdala processes emotionally salient stimuli, especially threat detection and fear conditioning.

questions.question: Surgical bilateral removal of the hippocampus leads to which severe clinical deficit?

options.text: Inability to form new declarative long-term memories (anterograde amnesia)
Total loss of long-term procedural muscle memories

questions.explanation: Hippocampal damage prevents consolidation of new episodic and semantic information into long-term storage.

questions.question: The primary somatosensory cortex, responsible for processing sensations of touch and bodily position, is located in which lobe?
questions.explanation: The somatosensory cortex occupies the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe.

questions.question: Phineas Gage survived an iron rod piercing his frontal lobes. What was the most dramatic long-term change observed?

options.text: He lost all ability to produce speech
His personality shifted from conscientious to impulsive, irreverent, and emotionally unstable
He completely forgot his childhood identity

questions.explanation: Damage to his prefrontal cortex impaired executive control, emotional regulation, and social judgment.

questions.question: A stroke patient can comprehend spoken sentences effortlessly but speaks with immense effort in slow, halting, telegraphic words. Where is the lesion?

options.text: Broca's Area in the left frontal lobe
Wernicke's Area in the left temporal lobe

questions.explanation: Broca's aphasia involves non-fluent, effortful speech production with relatively intact comprehension.

questions.question: What is the dense fiber bundle that bridges and transmits communication between the two cerebral hemispheres?
questions.explanation: The corpus callosum contains over 200 million axonal fibers uniting the left and right hemispheres.

questions.question: What gland is known as the 'master gland' of the endocrine system because it releases hormones that stimulate other endocrine glands?
questions.explanation: The pituitary gland, under hypothalamic direction, orchestrates hormone release throughout the endocrine system.

questions.question: The brain's dynamic capacity to alter its neural connections and rewire itself following injury or learning is known as:
questions.explanation: Neuroplasticity describes structural and functional adaptations of synaptic networks over the lifespan.

questions.question: Scientific neuroimaging demonstrates that humans utilize approximately 100% of their brains over the course of daily functioning, thoroughly debunking the 10% myth.
questions.explanation: True. Brain imaging confirms nearly all areas of the brain show activity during complex everyday tasks.

questions.question: An antagonist drug works by stimulating synaptic vesicles to produce more neurotransmitters than normal.
questions.explanation: False. Antagonists block or inhibit receptor activation, rather than increasing neurotransmitter synthesis.
